pages.html:
Amy Plant and Anna Best - questions for 'Playtime' discussion

what did you think about the game, as a parallel space to life? And how does this relate to risk taking in art, gambling or religion?

Can you say something about the time and space designated by games?

Is the notion of participation important? why bring participation into Art?

Does the artist have a right to play with the viewer? How could art become a fair game?

Are games, art and religion considered to varying degrees to be either educational or merely a way to kill time?

Has accessibility got anything to do with the reasons behind curating Game Show?

Why do you think Art has become so bereft of participation and of notions of daily performance?

What is the difference between a game or gambling and just playing (make believe etc)?

pages.html:
Discussion between Amy Plant and Anna Best prior to 'Playtime'

anna: So where were we? Game show..........

amy: yep games and art and the relationship between games and art and art itself being a game and then we talked about breaking the rules and how art can function as a kind of breaking through the rules of certain things

anna: what rules? do think there are art rules? do you think that art breaks art rules - that art breaks life rules?

amy: I think both definitely. but maybe arts job is to break the rules of art before so in a sense it is playing the game in the right way - do you see what I mean? - its following the rules if on a lot of levels because artists cant really recreate art thats already been made - or they dont do that

anna: apart from ben brown - and theres probably loads of others

amy: exactly yeah there are but I dont know - thats hard isnt it

anna: but the rules of art are to break the rules actually. thats what one was brought up with as a fledgling artist at art school. its what this centurys all about in art isnt it I suppose but its more interesting the idea that you say about how you could break rules in art and then in life almost as if art is a kind of space like an antechamber in front of life or something and lifes the big room and theres this other big room attached to it where things can be done first? I dont know..
pages.caption: Camden Talks: Playtime

pages.html:
amy: yeah I spose there's things - cos I don't know I mean - art in general isn't that useful in life but it also takes its reference points from life and can then create something which twists life in some way or gives a different perspective maybe to other perspectives and im not saying that arts the only thing that does that because other creative forms do - but maybe that's what creativity is - I mean creativity is a very difficult word so........

anna: including all sorts like academia and research and bla bla bla

amy: exactly yeah but I think art has - in a way it doesn't have - the responsibility to represent things in the way that they really are such as a documentary would or a piece of research would you sort of take on board a certain amount of responsibility to....

anna: yes subjectivity is ok in art isn't it?

amy: it is yeah

anna: where as it's not - well it is more and more isn't it - things have changed from the idea that theres some hard core universe of truth knocking around. I don't think people really believe in that anymore although im sure that's what people are taught in school - terrifying thought

amy: yeah it's true
pages.caption: Camden Talks: Playtime

pages.html:
anna: I mean I wonder sometimes about the individual and subjectivity and the personal in art and in culture in general and how that seems to be a real reaction to any form of totalitarianism - where you've got a kind of system from on high being beamed down on you whether that's universal scientific truth or the idea of communism - it's like turning round and saying no way don't want that........

amy: pressure yeah

anna: .........idea of authority saying this is how things are that really fascinates me in general

amy: but do you also think that art has a kind of escapism in it as well which is quite similar to games possibly?

anna: yeah I spose I do. most art viewers if they're not artists are coming in their play time - I mean it's leisure time - they're coming to be entertained or learn something or enrich their experience or something arent they they're coming to see some art. definitely it's escapism it's escapism from the daily grind. I think for artists it's a bit different

amy: yeah it is the daily grind for artists

anna: yeah but looking at someone else's work properly is an escape into something else

amy: into someone elses world or the way that someones presented a world
pages.caption: Camden Talks: Playtime

pages.html:
anna: yeah I think when I look at art I probably am looking for their system, their motivation, their intention, the aim of the game in a way, yeah I'm trying to find out what's the aim of their game and then I can begin to enjoy their game. Sophie Calle may be a good example - what's she trying to do? I haven't looked round the show yet

amy: you don't when your here every week do you

anna: I haven't had a chance to escape yet but in general going to art shows I go to get into somebody elses way of looking for sure it's like taking drugs -in a (very harmless) way. but how do you feel about the games show in relation to the work your idea the curatorial concept your and andys thing and the artists how they're approaching it versus a regular picasso exhibition at the tate kind of thing I mean there's a definite difference in the approach

amy: what's the difference in approach?

anna: yeah there's a definite difference isn't there

amy: yeah there is absolutely and I think that one of the first motivations for making 'game show' was to explore another experiment in participation from the audience and because games are things which people touch and they're very involving things and they're also things that everybody can relate to on some level - but there are a lot of different ....
pages.caption: Camden Talks: Playtime

pages.html:
...... amy: so in a way it's almost like a - it's not like trick where you were turning art into real life as much as possible, because in a way games are a part of life ....... I'm thinking about traditional kinds of games or board games and things

anna: not video games

amy: no and that was another thing we were quite clear about a kind of low tech experience that we wanted for people and on some levels that also involves a certain amount of nostalgia maybe

anna: like bingo

amy: exactly yeah

anna: bingo's marketed on nostalgia dave said to me - it was interesting

amy: really? that's interesting

anna: yeah the guy shaun whos gonna come next weekend he said that first of all they've got this image of blue rinse ladies coming to play and they want to get rid of that. well they're in cinemas there's nostalgia all over the place, lots of the crowd who come are elderly and there's a whole vibe of nostalgia - to come back to the bingo hall - and they're also starting to market to gay populations via gay magazines etc.....
pages.caption: Camden Talks: Playtime

pages.html:
amy: oh really right

anna: .........and he was saying that it's those men who are going to bingo because it's so fem.......

amy: do you think that's because it's got a kit'sch.....?

anna: - kit'sch - feminine - nostalgic

amy: right

anna: also away from the heterosexual social scenarios you get in pubs and stuff where if a woman goes out on her own theres no way shed be left in peace and stuff like that so it's like both women and gay men are getting away from that sort of quite aggressive on the pull........

anna: kind of culture

anna: whatever ........stuff - I thought that was quite interesting theres a real atmosphere theres safety - comfort - games. games are safe

amy: they are but they can be dangerous as well

anna: do you think?

amy: well those kinds of games are safe the kind of traditional games that you play you know in the parlour
pages.caption: Camden Talks: Playtime

pages.html:
anna: mind games - very scary

amy: but mind games are very dangerous yeah and I thought about that a lot when we were doing game show as well the idea of mind games and this idea of tricking people........

anna: oh trickery

amy: .........and in a sense I felt that some of the games that were produced had an element of that to them because there was something quite frustrating about them - well of some of the games on some levels for example - the chess set sedric christie made he decided that all the pieces would look the same so that it would make it very difficult to play and youd have to concentrate harder because the pieces were snooker balls and he had engraved on the snooker balls the names of the pieces. and all the snooker balls were the same colour so you didnt chose to be black or white you chose to be this way round or that way round if you see what I mean so there was this sort of - actually one comment that someone made was (before we started to do this game show and it was just an embryonic thing) was he basically said I don't think that artists can make as good games as the games that already exist that are made by people who do it for a living

anna: who said that?

amy: david thorp he said that

anna: oh right
pages.caption: Camden Talks: Playtime

pages.html:
amy: not to us directly he said that to someone else and the message got passed on to us which I thought was quite like - maybe they cant. but I thought that what maybe they could do was to twist the idea of what a game is or make one think more about what a game could be or how......... it depends because........ I suppose the chess set was an appropriated game. sedrick took an existing game. it was the same with the fruit machine where the winning signs or whatever become words and phrases that are not always pleasant....... or they might make you laugh.

anna: appropriating existing games

amy: yeah what I found quite interesting was on a lot of levels the chess set worked - I was quite worried about the chess set to begin with but I found almost everyone that actually played it - and people did sit down and actually play the game........

anna: david played yeah

amy: .........almost everyone that did played with someone that theyd never met before and this was another really important element to the show was this idea of slowing down and almost creating a space for....... for leisure almost or for stopping and that was another very deliberate reason for not having high tech things in there because it was very much about being situated in an urban context

anna: and making this space where you could have time to meet someone you didnt know
pages.caption: Camden Talks: Playtime

pages.html:
amy: yeah and have a different kind of interaction and the games are almost a catalyst for that to occur in and it's something that maybe were very good at doing when were children but when we get older I don't know

anna: barriers go up you only play games with people you know and like or life just gets more like that

amy: yeah it does

anna: playgrounds are fascinating locations arent they

amy: yeah they are

anna: I live opposite one and I watch the kids (like some creepy old creep) I just sit there watching them cos they're amazing I mean they're just darting around and they're in little groups and they're splitting up from their groups and going off and it's like homonymous bosh painting just with this big field with all these people all over it just doing totally different things in their own worlds and doing that kind of what's that the - that funny game - the hands clapping

amy: yeah what do you call it

anna: I mean when I did the hand clapping thing and cats cradle at school we knew they were really old fashioned and really there was this....... I think that's really interesting as well what you're say about theres this nostalgia in games
pages.caption: Camden Talks: Playtime

pages.html:
amy: yeah and they get handed down don't they and although they might change slightly as they go on there are some games that don't - yeah - and the origins of them are probably really fascinating - maybe like nursery rhymes

anna: ring-a-ring a-roses type of thing

amy: I don't know maybe/maybenot I don't know or something like hop scotch I don't know the history of hop scotch but I can imagine it having a purpose at some point

anna: yes definitely yes that's what thomas was talking about - games as a way of teaching about religion like snakes and ladders. it was a way of teaching children about heaven and hell

amy: wow

anna: if you're naughty you slither down snake and he was saying how at one point their mouths were at top of the snake and I think now they're at the bottom I may be wrong but I think it was inverted at one point to make it less scary or less literal maybe

amy: yeah sure

anna: cos snakes are pretty evil all in all arent they

amy: yeah and they can kill you - ladders are generally access things
pages.caption: Camden Talks: Playtime

pages.html:
anna: jacobs ladder going to heaven and stuff - so im sure hop scotch and things like that.......

amy: and chess was about war

anna: strategy

amy: yeah exactly

anna: ........so games - like art - are always about something else as well maybe they are and they arent

amy: and I think what was nice about game show as well was to have all the games that we had in there quite different in terms of how they were played and where they come from so we had the chess which was very traditional we had the fruit machine which is more of a modern invention and is more about gambling and so

anna: your on your own playing it very particularly

amy: exactly it's a sort of solitary experience. the boat race was more of an invented game in a way

anna: it was very child like. it was like a game of the very narrative games you play when you're a child where you have a camp. we used to have one which was the duvet put on top of an armchair on one side and god knows what on the other and that was just wild.
pages.caption: Camden Talks: Playtime

pages.html:
anna:.....that sort of instant narrative that goes on spaced over time as well like from one saturday to the next you might play the same game with the same people as a kid do you remember doing that? I remember doing that

amy: yeah I do remember doing that

anna: having a game that wasnt a board game it was our game

amy: yeah make believe games and you maybe had characters and roles within those games - in your games?

anna: oh yeah absolutely we played starski and hutch and I was starski

amy: and they go on for hours don't they? amazing

anna: yeah hours - hours of pretending not to be who you are or discovering - or trying to discover who you are as a child I suppose arent you? you're putting on different hats - I mean erica's thing wasnt like that but it was a bit like that wasnt it?

amy: in the way in that it was quite make believe but it was also about competition as well cos it was a race and there was definitely a winner and the idea that if you wanted to you could get into trying to make the winning boat - you know which was quite nice and actually the winning boat was......

anna: whose was the winning boat do you know?
pages.caption: Camden Talks: Playtime

pages.html:
amy: ......it was david salbys who is a friend and he had actually made a boat that was specifically designed to go fast and it was a real goer it was faster than anyone elses

anna: wow god

amy: he did it twice before the whole race had finished. but also the other interesting thing about race is the background of it

anna: which was the title of the piece wasnt it?

amy: yeah it was also the title of the piece so it had a kind of double meaning and the coloured paper that erica chose (that was available for people to make their boats with) all the colours were based on victorian classifications of race - so like brown would be west indian/indian, yellow obviously japan/china, white obviously and red and black so they were the colours - and it was interesting when we actually went down to the canal and everybody was launching their boat she was doing things like letting the whites go last and that kind of thing she would say throw in the red ones now and shed also written text along the canal - along the actual length of the race - which had actually been marked out and related to these ideas. so that was really the only point that those things came out in an obvious way and I quite like that as well and that's very similar to games as we were saying before

anna: education?
pages.caption: Camden Talks: Playtime

pages.html:
amy: yeah education but in a very kind of subtle way and that unless you go into it you don't actually understand the origins of it - all blind text in a way

anna: it's like some patterns having a meaning originally and then they travel and you don't know what the meaning of your brixton-african textile is any more or whatever.

amy: exactly yeah

anna: that's interesting in relation to bingo because of the whole colours thing. I had a chat to carol last week about how people chose different coloured pens to dab their bingo books with and they chose a yellow pen to go with the page of the bingo book that's red partly visually so you can see it better but also just to do with pattern making. I mean there were some weird things going on like the desire to complete this pattern to fill in the form - play the game/weird cross word thing and there was something quite interesting about these frames like cross word or bingo book or lottery card that you see it and you just want to fill it in or to tick the box - it's a very weird level of participation

amy: it is because it's very premeditated and there isn't a huge amount of room there for changing that system or applying your own meaning onto the thing - and it's not necessary really because that isn't the idea - but you see maybe if an artist was given a lottery ticket or a bingo card to do what - to make a piece of work out of - what would they do?
pages.caption: Camden Talks: Playtime

pages.html:
amy:..... maybe they'd break that rule of filling in the box you're supposed to fill in and then perhaps it would become something else. but talking about participation that's something im quite interested in because there are a lot of art pieces which (and im not saying that I think game show addressed this in any way at all because I don't think it did) but there are a lot of art pieces that invite participation from the audience but only on a level of pressing a button or maybe switching something on or touching something and that is meant to be interactive

anna: oh no I completely agree with you it makes me want to throw up

amy: it's really really pathetic and patronising

anna: when you hear people say they're making interactive art and you kind of go umhum what? what's it like? and when you go into the room a laser beam triggers a video and you just think interactive?

amy: interactive?

anna: for god's sake it's almost like multi medias been taken over by a certain part of the industry

amy: yes sure
pages.caption: Camden Talks: Playtime

pages.html:
anna: you cant say multi media anymore without it - it means specifics work on computers doesn't it? and interactive is being used as well by the computer culture/industry whatever - theyve stolen it

amy: they have

anna: theyve kind of turned it into not meaning what it should mean

amy: so participation would be a more useful word for art works which invite the audience to join in

anna: but games did address participation - no?

amy: it did address participation but what worries me is actually allowing the audience/participants/whateveryouwanttocallthem/customers even - clients

anna: clients

amy: yeah yeah - to actually give them the space to create their own meaning in a sense and in some way that did happen as we were saying before about the space being open enough to for you and david to make that piece on the floor or for people to make their own games

anna: did they?
pages.caption: Camden Talks: Playtime

pages.html:
amy: yeah that happened. there were times when we just discovered some thing that someone had left behind to contribute which was really really nice cos we also brought ordinary games in as well so it sort of grew and some people brought things - well erica one of the artists she brought a book of party games - so it kind of grew and so it wasnt just the art works at the end

anna: it was kind of like blur at the end I mean in a really nice way

amy: it was blur yes and it was deliberate blur you know there was a point to it and it was interesting because after wed finished putting all the work in the space we sat back and said this looks too clean - basically it looked too much like another exhibition and it was not the kind of atmosphere that we wanted because I think if you're inviting people to participate then they have to feel comfortable on some level

anna: it's like - what messages do you get when you walk into a space? if it's too much like an art gallery then the messages you get - which is fine but they're like watch look look but don't touch and talk if you have to - quietly

amy: but really you're supposed to contemplate this thing in a quite a spiritual way

anna: yeah which is fine but may not be appropriate
pages.caption: Camden Talks: Playtime

pages.html:
amy: the that way we organised the space was in a sense our interpretation if you see what I mean

anna: we as curators?

amy: curators yeah

anna: your interpretation of the work or of the concept - of the original.....

amy: of all of it in a sense cos all of the work was designed for people to join in - none of the artists just made a piece and we wouldn't just take a piece which we thought oh this would be good

anna: specially made for the show

amy: not all of it was specially made for the show but it was all specially made for people to play with and that was really important - that we couldn't have anything in there that the artists were precious over and that was one of the key things about that show was a non-possessiveness over it and I think then you allow new meanings to come in and evolve because it's growing - and the audience was really important for that - the show would not have worked without an audience it would be nothing with out people coming in and playing it would have been nothing

anna: meaningless
pages.caption: Camden Talks: Playtime

pages.html:
amy: yeah they created the meaning

anna: yeah and they knew that

amy: they knew that yeah

anna: one felt that was the case it was like yes being invited to get involved.......

amy: im sure there are things we could have done to improve that - that's quite common but it would be quite interesting to talk about

anna: big work is that how in each particular context each thing

amy: .........and I think one of the most rewarding things about it was the amount of children that got involved. they were coming in every day that we were open - local children - and hanging out

anna: ella really made friends with some of the children round there hasnt she?

amy: yeah she has. so I think for her it was really important in terms of building up a relationship on a local level with some of the people around and the fact that the kids felt they could just come in and hang out - I mean everybody did - every body that came spent time. which was another really important thing.
pages.caption: Camden Talks: Playtime

pages.html:
anna:... we thought about that a lot and that's why we served tea and cocktails because we wanted people to spend time. so often you go in to see art wiz round you don't actually spend time and that was very important to that idea of actually slowing down and having the space to relax

anna: yeah I really like that

amy: so slowing down was a very important part of the whole concept and even the boat race was slow it was a slow race and in that sense it was really beautiful

anna: you couldn't get an instant hit or an instant - yeah it was very un instant

amy: yeah and I think that's quite important I think that's something that we.....

anna: it's a process isn't it. games playing is a process by definition or something. one of the nice things that's come up at the bingo - one woman I spoke to said quite particularly that she doesn't look at what the prize money is while shes playing because she doesn't want to know what prize money she might win or lose ......

amy: that's interesting
pages.caption: Camden Talks: Playtime

pages.html:
anna: ......which is really odd it's like - why are you playing bingo then? cos I thought the whole thing was that you get this buzz (and im sure it is for most people) you get this buzz that you might win a hundred quid it starts off at ten pounds but when ive been there - (ive never seen the national game but im going there tonight to see that and that gets really lots of money) yeah so I was really intrigued and it was like why do you? and she just enjoys playing, the social thing and just being there and yeah it was much a richer amount of reasons than I had initially associated with going to bingo - I mean theres so many more facets

amy: than winning money

anna: theres much more happening there than youd think at first and so do you play to win or do you play as well to just play and most em say both. if you just want to win you play the fruit machines and a lot of people do go and spend what theyve just won at bingo on the fruit machines they're very strategically placed right by the doors

amy: so that's the first thing they see

anna: and that's how the company make money - on the machines not on bingo (so they say)

amy: that's interesting

anna: well it's cut throat it's a business it's an interesting one. did you talk to people who came to race about why they like to play games or did you get any thoughts on that

pages.html:
amy: no not really

anna: like why do we play games? is it more than slow......

amy: oh it's definitely more than just a leisure thing I think I think theres a lot more involved than that and I think theres a lot of pleasure in winning even if it's not winning money but winning chess or winning.... and also some of them are mind expanders almost or brain exercises like a crossword or even like chess and I think a lot of people really enjoy that and it keeps their brain - exercising the muscles of the brain so I think that's another reason

anna: I've never quite got the my head around that

amy: yeah I never play chess and.......

anna: I hate -

amy: ...... cross words I'm terrible at them

anna: yeah - quiz shows on telly I'm just kind of

amy: well quiz shows are another thing

pages.html:
anna: I think you need - well do you think you need a particular type of brain for some games over others

anna: theres information - some brains seem very capable - I mean some brains seem really good at numbers some brains seem particularly good at holding onto information - I don't have either of those brains

amy: no I don't either

amy: I don't know

anna: mush brain

amy: art brain - the lush brain - the mush brain

anna: maybe we've got visual brains? I think so. I think I'm more connected to visual things than to logical things like numbers and im also really bad at things like telling my left from my right things like that yeah I don't know why that is but.......

amy: yeah it is interesting I mean I literally feel like I just have not got the time or the space to remember information it's like sorry I can't you know I just can't fit it in
pages.caption: Camden Talks: Playtime

pages.html:
anna: yeah no it's amazing. people get addicted to those quiz shows as well there was a really interesting programme

amy: my dad's schizophrenic and he was a scientologist before he was schizophrenic which is interesting and now he's more into buddhism but when he is ill - cos he goes through phases of when he stops taking medication and stuff-

anna: in and out? does he go into hospital and stuff?

amy: yeah he stayed with me when he was really ill for a couple of weeks and during that time he was writing a lot. he was writing his own rules. he always used to talk to me about life being a game when I was really little I really remember it really clearly and his rules are for how people should live. he thinks hes king of england when hes ill

anna: my brother thought he was father christmas when he was ill. that's a big archetype
pages.caption: Camden Talks: Playtime

pages.html:
amy: yeah and a lot of people think they're jesus or elvis or

anna: virgin mary

amy: and it's quite interesting how they become icons in a way

anna: and so do people around them I don't know if you've had that sort experience.. I've had a friend who went manic and she sort of designated me as her guardian angel and she then went off to be pretty destructive... In her guardian angels life it was quite weird being told by someone that they'd met the virgin mary in the shop down the road and you're their guardian angel I felt very... yeah... it was very frightening. I felt very responsible I'd been made to be to feel responsible

amy: and that's a kind of transference thing I think on behalf of that person that they

anna: what do mean? you mean that they put it onto someone else? yeah in a way I mean it's also obviously someone who had a lot of respect for you so it's also like maybe an expression of that

anna: oh yeah, mmmm
pages.caption: Camden Talks: Playtime

pages.html:
amy: but my dad also thinks that everyone in our family, cos he believes in reincarnation, so he believes that everyone - but I was alice in wonderland which is quite interesting and he used to make books for me of alice in wonderland a kind of alternative alice in wonderland and my brother was ceasar. his dad was the king of england of course

anna: as well

amy: well yeah but he got adopted of course and my nan was an actress and he knows that because he saw a picture of her in the library

anna: and what about your mum?

amy: well she doesn't really come into it

anna: she wasnt characterised or something

amy: no

anna: that is really interesting cos I think people - whether sane or insane they do it all the time they kind of characterise or categorise

amy: well people definitely put people on pedestals

anna: and fit people into systems......
pages.caption: Camden Talks: Playtime

pages.html:
amy: yeah

anna: ......that they have. they have their own systems and they fit......

amy: that's interesting

anna: I mean that's what our society is, it's a kind of social system isn't it. I mean when you go out with someone you fit them into that slot don't you and you both fit with in that or something else

amy: yeah it's almost like there are these boxes laid out for us where we can put different aspects of our lives - like filing

anna: and you put those feelings and that activity into that person and you call it a love affair or a business relationship or whatever - very odd some how

amy: and im quite interested in blurring those as well cos I don't necessarily find them particularly useful to me personally

anna: no I think they're limiting but then what do you do with em? what do you do? not you personally but what does one do I mean do you make a knew system

amy: not necessarily no I think you just become more open... like the system can maybe have lots of different doors in it so if you imagine it as you know what I mean a system where people can go in and out and .....
pages.caption: Camden Talks: Playtime

pages.html:
anna: be more than one thing

amy: .......and if you let the things be where they want to be with in the system rather than you necessarily categorising them that's being natural isn't it? just seeing what things are like in a natural way and if they cross over and there's comfortableness with that then why not let that happen

anna: yeah I guess that takes a certain amount of courage and within the realm of normality we're expected to have a certain amount of courage to do that. I think when people are very ill they set up millions of barriers and categorisations

amy: yeah yeah maybe they do

anna: I need to read again about this guy donald crowhurst did I mention him to you ever?

amy: did you mention him last week? no, you didn't mention him. - end -
